name: Catharism
info: Catharism was a Christian dualist movement of Occitania and northern Italy between the 12th and 14th centuries, whose Good Christians were attacked by the Albigensian Crusade and the Inquisition; scholars still debate how far it existed as an organised religion.

facts.origin: the Rhineland, northern France, the Languedoc and northern Italy in the 12th century, first reported at Cologne in 1143; whether it came from the Byzantine Empire or arose locally is debated
facts.founder: none: it was taught at first by ascetic leaders who set few guidelines, and Catholic writers named it from outside
facts.scriptures: the New Testament, the Bogomil Gospel of the Secret Supper, a modified Ascension of Isaiah and The Book of the Two Principles; few Cathar texts survive, as most were destroyed
facts.followers: none: the Inquisition, which claimed to have eradicated Catharism by 1350, ended it; the Languedoc's last known Perfect was executed in 1321

t: Known mostly from Catholic opponents, the Cathars are described as holding that a good God of the spiritual realm stood against an evil god who made the material world, in which souls were trapped until released by the consolamentum.

The Albigensian Crusade, begun in 1209, and then the Inquisition, set up in 1233, ended the movement; thousands were killed, among them the people of Béziers and more than 200 Perfects burned at Montségur in 1244.

Since the 1990s some historians, notably R. I. Moore, have questioned whether Catharism was an organised religion at all, while others hold that the evidence shows a real heresy with a theology of its own.
dyk: On 13 May 1239 in Champagne, 183 men and women convicted of Catharism were burned at the stake on the orders of the Dominican inquisitor Robert le Bougre, himself a former Cathar Perfect.
ev: Eberwin of Steinfeld reports at Cologne the first confirmed group with beliefs like those later called Cathar
A council at Saint-Félix-Lauragais is attended by the Bogomil papa Nicetas, the Cathar bishop of northern France and a Lombard leader
The papal legate Pierre de Castelnau is murdered, and Pope Innocent III orders a crusade preached against the Cathars
The crusaders besiege Béziers on 22 July, and its inhabitants are massacred
The Treaty of Paris ends the official war and strips the House of Toulouse and the Trencavels of their fiefs
The Inquisition is established to uproot the remaining Cathars
Montségur falls, and over 200 Cathar Perfects are burned at the prat dels cremats
Guillaume Bélibaste, the last known Cathar perfect in the Languedoc, is executed

sections.origins:
The origins of Cathar beliefs are unclear. Most 20th-century historians agreed that they came from the East along trade routes from the Byzantine Empire, and that the movement was greatly influenced by the Bogomils of the First Bulgarian Empire, perhaps through Paulicians resettled in Thrace. Mark Pegg and others warn against inferring direct historical links from similarities that modern scholars perceive. Dimitri Obolensky and Steven Runciman proposed descent from Manichaeism and early Gnostic movements; this view has been widely rejected since primary Manichaean texts were found, though traditional Catholic scholarship still associates the Cathars with Manichaeism.

Most scholars agree that identifiable Catharism did not emerge before 1143, when the cleric Eberwin of Steinfeld reported a group with similar beliefs at Cologne. A council held in 1167 at Saint-Félix-Lauragais was attended by local figures, the Bogomil papa Nicetas, the Cathar bishop of northern France and a leader of the Cathars of Lombardy.

The present debate has two frameworks: transmission through the Byzantine Empire, argued by Malcolm Barber and Janet and Bernard Hamilton, or an independent local Latin Christian development unrelated to any dualist heresy, argued by Robert Ian Moore and Mark Gregory Pegg.
sections.beliefs:
Few Cathar texts survive, so most of what is known comes from Catholic denunciations. According to them, Cathars believed in two Gods: the good God of Heaven, creator of the spiritual realm, and an evil god, often called Rex Mundi, who made the visible world. Some communities held a mitigated dualism in which Satan was once the true God’s servant; others, probably a majority over time, held an absolute dualism of two equal powers. Human souls were seen as angels seduced by Satan and trapped in matter, reincarnated until they renounced the material self.

Cathars venerated Jesus and called themselves Good Christians, but denied his physical incarnation and resurrection; authors compare their view with Docetism. They rejected the cross as an instrument of torture, saw the New Testament’s resurrection as a symbol of reincarnation, and denied transubstantiation, purgatory and prayers to saints. Some communities expected a Day of Judgment.

Their one central rite was the consolamentum, which removed all sin and made the believer a Perfect. They ate no meat, cheese, eggs or milk, as products of sexual intercourse, but ate fish, believed to arise by spontaneous generation. War and capital punishment were condemned, and reproduction was seen as a moral evil.
sections.texts:
Few writings of the Cathars survive, because most were destroyed after the Papacy judged their doctrine a threat, and so the record rests mainly on their opponents. Beside the New Testament, their alleged sacred texts included the Bogomil Gospel of the Secret Supper, also called John’s Interrogation, and a modified version of the Ascension of Isaiah. They regarded the Old Testament as written by Satan, apart from a few books they accepted, and read the Book of Revelation not as prophecy but as an allegorical chronicle of Satan’s rebellion.

One large Cathar work survives, The Book of Two Principles (Liber de duobus principiis), possibly written by the Italian Cathar John Lugio of Bergamo. It sets out dualist theology from the viewpoint of some Albanenses Cathars. A few other texts survive in their opponents’ hands, such as the Rituel Cathare de Lyon. The Cathars held that scripture should be read in the vernacular.

The Fournier Register, made when Jacques Fournier, Bishop of Pamiers, had suspected heretics interrogated around Montaillou, records their words through scribes. It was edited by Jean Duvernoy and is the basis of Emmanuel Le Roy Ladurie’s Montaillou.
sections.spread:
Cathars sprang up in the Rhineland cities, particularly Cologne, and in northern France in the mid-12th century, and in the Languedoc and northern Italian cities in the mid to late 12th century. In the Languedoc and northern Italy they attained their greatest popularity. By 1207 many towns of Provence and its vicinity were almost wholly Cathar. Missions sent from 1147, among them those of Bernard of Clairvaux and of Henry of Marcy, won only momentary successes.

In January 1208 the legate Pierre de Castelnau was murdered, and Pope Innocent III ordered a crusade preached. The Albigensian Crusade lasted twenty years. At Béziers, besieged on 22 July 1209, crusaders killed at least 7,000 people according to reports, though some scholars dispute the number. Arnaud Amalric wrote that twenty thousand were put to the sword, a figure scholars dispute as figurative. At Muret in 1213 Simon de Montfort defeated the allied army of Raymond of Toulouse and Peter II of Aragon, who died there. The Treaty of Paris of 1229 ended the war.

The Inquisition, established in 1233, crushed Catharism as a popular movement. Over 200 Perfects were burned at Montségur on 16 March 1244. Peire Autier, leader of a revival in the Pyrenean foothills, was executed in 1310, and the last known Perfect of the Languedoc, Guillaume Bélibaste, in 1321.
sections.community:
Cathars called themselves Good Men, Good Women or Good Christians; the name Cathar was coined by Catholic theologians, and whether the movement used it is debated. It is alleged that the Languedoc church had a flat structure, with the Perfecti, whom they called bonhommes, and unbaptised believers, the credentes. Bishoprics were created at Albi around 1165, then at Toulouse, Carcassonne and Agen, four by 1200, and Razès about 1225. Perfecti lived austerely and travelled in pairs.

Women could be Perfects and administer the consolamentum, so Catharism has been seen as giving women the greatest opportunities for independent action. Women Perfects had their own houses, and communal homes taught women the faith. Yet some Cathars held that salvation required a last incarnation as a man, and the late Cathars of France began to exclude women Perfects, though Italian Perfects still included them.

The Cathars had little hostility to Jews and appointed some as bailiffs and public officials. When Bishop Fulk of Toulouse rebuked the Languedoc knights for not pursuing heretics, they replied that they had been reared among them and had relatives among them. Repentant lay believers were spared but had to sew yellow crosses onto their clothing; those who refused to recant or relapsed were hanged or burned.
sections.legacy:
Since the 1990s the existence of Catharism as an institutional religion has been contested. R. I. Moore argues in The War on Heresy that it was largely contrived in the imaginations of churchmen from scattered local anticlericalism and a broader spiritual revival, and some scholars have called the fear of Cathars a moral panic comparable with the witch-hunts. Claire Taylor and Rebecca Rist reply that evidence shows a real heresy, and Lucy Sackville argues that it had an organised theology. Cathars in Question (2016), edited by Antonio Sennis, gathered the conflicting views.

Later readers reinterpreted the Cathars. John Foxe and Jean Duvernoy saw proto-Protestant theology in them, a reading many historians criticised, and some 20th-century Baptists claimed them as forerunners, which Dwight Longenecker rejects and Baptist historiography has largely left. In the 1930s Otto Rahn linked them to the Holy Grail, and popular culture has linked them to the Knights Templar. The Waldensians, who suffered persecution in the same area, survive today.

Today the Cathar castles of Montségur and Carcassonne stand in what the Aude calls Pays cathare. The Occitan song Lo Boièr is particularly associated with Catharism, and its legacy is also seen in the troubadours’ poems and songs.

summary: Catharism was a Christian dualist movement of the Rhineland, the Languedoc and northern Italy from the 12th to the 14th century, known mostly through Catholic accounts. It was attacked by the Albigensian Crusade from 1209 and by the Inquisition, which claimed to have eradicated it by 1350. Historians still debate how organised it was.
references: Malcolm Barber, The Cathars: Dualist heretics in Languedoc in the High Middle Ages (Longman, 2000)
Malcolm Lambert, Medieval Heresy: Popular Movements from the Gregorian Reform to the Reformation (Blackwell, 2002)
Emmanuel Le Roy Ladurie, Montaillou: Cathars and Catholics in a French Village, 1294–1324 (Penguin, 1990)
R. I. Moore, The War on Heresy (Profile Books, 2012)
notes: Dates: start 1143 circa (the article says identifiable Catharism did not emerge until at least 1143, Eberwin of Steinfeld at Cologne). End 1350 circa: the Inquisition 'claimed to have eradicated them by 1350'; the article also says the Languedoc survival lasted 'up to around 1325' and that few Inquisition proceedings follow 1330. Bélibaste 1321 is its date for the last Languedoc Perfect (the article's lede-level 1350 and the 1325 differ slightly).

The article's Genocide subsection is empty; I did not use the word. The article's Etymology section holds a rhetorical passage ('Whether they acted in defense…') and a long note on the earlier 'Cathari' (Novatians, Augustine's Catharistas); both left out.

Béziers: 7,000 and 20,000 are given with the article's own caveats; the 'Kill them all' quotation (reported thirty years later by a non-witness) is left out. The endura and the smothering claim are left out as extreme and doubtful.

The article names 1208 for Castelnau's murder (January 1208) and orders the crusade after it; event 1208 combines both. 1213 Muret is in the text only. Montségur massacre called 'over 200 Cathar Perfects' as the article says.
References are left empty: the article's lists are empty in the saved text.
